region: Guianas, lower Amazon & Rio Negro — Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana & Brazil
description: The hardiest pencilfish, living among dense vegetation in slow streams and floodplain lakes. Males spread their red, white-tipped lower fins at rivals, and at night the bold stripe breaks up into dark blotches.

region: Amazon basin & Rio Negro — Brazil, Colombia & Peru; also Guyana
description: Hangs among floating plants at a 45° head-up angle, picking tiny invertebrates from just below the surface. Its dark band sweeps down into the black lower tail lobe, giving the "hockey stick" outline; at night it shows dark blotches instead.

region: Amazon, Rio Negro & Orinoco basins — Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela & Guyana
description: Like the hockeystick pencilfish it rests head-up beneath floating plants. A single black band edged with gold runs from the snout into the lower caudal lobe, which carries a red-and-white blaze in males.

region: Amazon & Rio Negro basins and the Guianas — Brazil, Peru, Colombia & Guyana
description: A blackwater species of flooded forest and vegetated margins, marked by three dark lines and red flashes at the base of each fin. A micropredator that needs small live or frozen foods to colour up fully.

region: Guianas, lower Amazon & Rio Negro — Suriname, Guyana, French Guiana, Brazil, Colombia & Peru
description: One of the smallest and stockiest pencilfish, with three black stripes and a ruby-red band. Pairs scatter a few eggs among fine-leaved plants and will eat them if given the chance.

region: Peruvian Amazon — Nanay & lower Marañón drainages near Iquitos
description: Described in 2001 from fish exported through Iquitos, Peru; males are the most intensely red of all pencilfish. Dominant males hold small spaces among plants and display to each other with spread red, white-tipped fins.

region: Guyana — Demerara River basin
description: Also called the blackstripe pencilfish: a slender, comparatively large species of shaded, slow-flowing Guyanese streams, with a broad black band edged above in gold and red at the base of the tail. Like its relatives it rests among plants at night in a blotched night livery.

region: Guyana — Mazaruni River drainage
description: Unique among pencilfish in replacing the lateral stripe with five comma-shaped black bars on a golden body. Also called Espe's pencilfish, it lives in tannin-stained forest streams and is a peaceful midwater shoaler.

region: Peruvian Amazon — Loreto
description: A small pencilfish from Peruvian forest streams, described in 2009 and named for the bright red tail fin of adults. It shows the classic golden body crossed lengthwise by a bold black band.

region: Guyana and the Amazon & Rio Negro basins of Brazil
description: A small, slender pencilfish with two dark stripes: a broad band along the midline and a narrower one low on the flank. It lives among leaf litter and plants in slow blackwater streams; males show red in the anal and tail fins.

region: Suriname, Guyana, French Guiana & the lower Amazon, Brazil
description: Named for its two black stripes; the lower one runs along the flank above a bright white belly. Males carry red at the base of the tail fin and bluish-white tips on the pelvic fins.

region: Upper Rio Negro & upper Orinoco — Brazil & Venezuela
description: At about 2 cm the smallest pencilfish, found among submerged vegetation in acidic blackwater streams. Males show a bright red anal fin and red below the black lateral stripe.

region: Guianas & lower Amazon — Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana & Pará, Brazil
description: Famous for spawning out of water: a pair leaps together to stick eggs to an overhanging leaf, and the male splashes them with his tail at regular intervals until they hatch two to three days later.

region: Central Amazon, Rio Negro & upper Orinoco — Brazil & Venezuela
description: Long sold as Copella nattereri, this small blackwater Copella has a reddish-brown spot on each flank scale, forming neat rows. Unlike the splash tetra it spawns on submerged leaves, where the male guards and fans the eggs.

region: Rio Negro & middle Amazon — Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela & Peru
description: Each scale on the flank bears a dark red dot, giving the "beautiful-scaled characin" look of its other common name. Eggs are laid on a submerged leaf or stone and guarded by the male.

region: Middle & upper Amazon basin — Brazil & Peru
description: A robust lebiasinid whose silvery-blue flanks are dotted with a red spot on each scale. Unusually for a characin, the male digs a shallow pit in sand where the eggs are laid, then guards and fans them.

region: Lower Paraná & Uruguay basins — Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay & Uruguay
description: Also called Rachow's pyrrhulina, a subtropical species of quiet, vegetated waters. The female lays eggs on a broad leaf the male has cleaned, and he guards the clutch, fanning water over it with his fins.

region: Upper Paraná, Paraguay & Mamoré basins — Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay & Argentina
description: A small, hardy Pyrrhulina often sold as P. rachoviana, with a dark line from the snout through the eye and red-dotted flanks. Males clean a leaf for spawning and guard the eggs until they hatch.

region: Amazon, Rio Negro & Orinoco basins — Brazil, Peru, Colombia & Venezuela
description: Its dark line from the snout through the eye stops just behind the gill cover, giving the "short-lined" name. It lives in shallow forest streams and floodplain pools, where males guard eggs laid on leaves.

region: Amazon basin — Peru, Colombia & Brazil
description: Recognised by a broad black band from the snout through the eye to about mid-body, and a black spot in the dorsal fin. A shy, slender species of shaded forest streams that spawns on submerged leaves.

region: Pacific slope of Ecuador & northern Peru
description: A robust lebiasinid from coastal rivers west of the Andes, named for its two dark spots: a humeral spot behind the head and another at the tail base, with a bright red spot just behind the first. Far larger and more predatory than its pencilfish relatives, it hunts insects and small fish.

region: Amazon basin & the Guianas — Peru, Colombia, Brazil, Guyana, Suriname & French Guiana
description: Lives right under the surface of forest streams; its deep keel holds the muscles that power wing-like pectoral fins, and startled shoals skitter and leap clear of the water. Feeds almost entirely on insects that fall onto the surface.

region: Orinoco, Rio Negro & upper Amazon — Venezuela, Colombia, Brazil, Peru & Bolivia
description: A blackwater hatchetfish whose common name comes from the dark bases of its pectoral "wings"; a black line also edges its keel. Like all hatchetfish it hunts insects at the surface and leaps clear of the water when alarmed.

region: Upper Amazon — Peru & Bolivia
description: The smallest hatchetfish at about 2.5 cm: a translucent, silvery fish of shaded upper Amazon streams. Delicate and very skittish, it needs calm water, floating cover and a tight lid.

region: Upper Amazon — Peru, Colombia, Brazil & Bolivia
description: Also called Scherer's hatchetfish, a small, yellowish and translucent species with faint dark marbling on the keel. It shoals beneath floating vegetation in quiet, shaded water.

region: Guianas & Amazon basin — Guyana, Suriname, Brazil, Peru & Bolivia
description: A sturdy silver hatchetfish with a dark midlateral line bordered above by a bright silver one. It shoals just below the surface of rivers and floodplain lakes, snapping up insects and leaping when chased.

region: Lower Amazon basin — Pará, Brazil
description: Very like the common hatchetfish but confined to the lower Amazon; a bright silver species with a thin dark line along the flank. Shoals feed on insects trapped in the surface film.

region: Panama, Colombia & Venezuela — Pacific and Caribbean drainages
description: Rows of dark spots and short bars mark its silver-gray body. It ranges further north than other hatchetfish, into Panama, living in slow rivers and swamps on both sides of the isthmus.

region: Amazon, Orinoco & Paraná–Paraguay basins — Venezuela to Argentina
description: The deepest-chested hatchetfish, platinum-silver with a black spot at the base of the dorsal fin. Shoals patrol just beneath the surface of rivers and lakes and leap clear of the water when pursued.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins — Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Venezuela & Bolivia
description: The largest hatchetfish, reaching about 9 cm, with a bright platinum body and a deep, blade-like keel. It shoals in open river channels and needs a long tank with plenty of surface swimming room.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins and the Guianas — Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela, Peru, Guyana & Suriname
description: A rheophilic headstander of rocky rapids that swims head-down, grazing algae and tiny invertebrates from crevices with its small upturned mouth. Often aggressive toward its own kind unless kept singly or in a sizeable group.

region: Orinoco, Essequibo & eastern Amazon tributaries — Venezuela, Guyana & Brazil
description: Smaller than the striped headstander, with two broad dark bands separated by narrow golden lines and much less red in its fins. It grazes algae and biofilm head-down from rocks in clear, flowing water.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins and the Guianas
description: A large, active anostomid banded with ten black bars on bright yellow; adults develop an orange-red throat. It eats plants voraciously and is a notorious jumper, needing a heavy lid and a large tank.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins
description: Often sold alongside L. fasciatus, from which it usually differs in having nine rather than ten black bars on its yellow body. A herbivorous grazer and a powerful jumper.

region: Northern & central South America — Orinoco, Amazon & Paraná–Paraguay basins
description: Banded lengthwise rather than across, with four black stripes on a cream-yellow body. A boisterous grazer of plants and detritus that shoals in the wild and needs robust tankmates.

region: Orinoco & Essequibo basins — Venezuela, Colombia & Guyana
description: Named for its red-orange lips and fins, set against a yellow body with three black lengthwise stripes. A large, active grazer that will destroy soft plants.

region: Guianas & northern Amazon — Suriname, Guyana, French Guiana & Brazil
description: Its yellow-tan flanks carry rows of large, rounded black spots rather than bands. Like other leporinus it grazes plants and algae and often swims slightly head-down.

region: Upper Paraná basin — southeastern Brazil
description: A subtropical leporinus from the upper Paraná system, yellow with eight bold black bars. Like its relatives it is a strong jumper and an enthusiastic plant-eater.

region: Amazon, Orinoco & Paraguay basins — Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Venezuela, Bolivia & Paraguay
description: A deep-backed headstander with a high, arched profile and irregular dark bands on gray-yellow. It browses algae, plants and small invertebrates head-down and becomes quarrelsome with its own kind as it matures.

region: Amazon, Rio Negro & Orinoco basins — Brazil, Colombia & Venezuela
description: A slender anostomid with a single broad black stripe from snout to tail on a silvery body. It forages head-down along wood and rocks for algae, detritus and small invertebrates.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins and the Guianas
description: A slender headstander, formerly placed in Anostomus, marked with three round black spots along the flank, the last at the base of the tail. It roots head-down in leaf litter and crevices for small invertebrates and algae.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins and the Guianas — Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Venezuela, Guyana & Suriname
description: A peaceful headstander that hovers nose-down among plants and roots, picking at algae, detritus and tiny invertebrates. Each scale carries a dark dot, forming neat rows, and a dark band runs from snout to tail.

region: Amazon, Essequibo & Paraná–Paraguay basins and coastal rivers of NE Brazil
description: Lives in loose shoals that protect it from dolphins, caimans and birds more than they help it hunt; much of its diet is fish fins, scales, insects and carrion. Skittish in aquaria, pairs dig a nest in the substrate and guard the eggs.

region: Orinoco basin — Venezuela & Colombia
description: The Orinoco's red-bellied piranha, distinguished by a large black spot behind the gill cover. It gathers in big shoals in the seasonally flooded llanos, scavenging and biting chunks from fish and other prey.

region: São Francisco basin — Brazil
description: Endemic to Brazil's São Francisco River, the largest Pygocentrus has a yellow-orange throat and belly. Heavier than the red-bellied piranha, it shoals in open river channels and reservoirs.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins and the Guianas
description: Also sold as the black piranha: the largest Serrasalmus, a solitary ambush hunter whose body darkens almost to black with age and whose eyes are a striking ruby red. It is cannibalistic and must be kept alone.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins — Brazil & Venezuela
description: A large, deep-bodied Serrasalmus whose silver flanks are densely flecked with dark spots under an iridescent sheen. Like most Serrasalmus it attacks tankmates and is kept alone.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins — Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Venezuela & Bolivia
description: An unusually slender, pointed-snouted piranha whose diet is dominated by fins and scales bitten from other fish. Highly aggressive even to its own kind, it is always kept alone.

region: Tocantins–Araguaia basin — Brazil
description: A medium-sized piranha of the Tocantins–Araguaia, unmistakable for the broad violet-black band that runs from the lower jaw up over the nape to the front of the dorsal fin. Like other Serrasalmus it is aggressive toward its own kind and is kept alone.

region: Upper Amazon — Peru, Bolivia & western Brazil
description: Also called Sanchez's piranha: a small, rhomboid Serrasalmus with a ruby-red throat and red eyes. Despite its modest size it is aggressive and best kept alone.

region: Orinoco, Essequibo & Rio Negro — Venezuela, Colombia, Guyana, Suriname & Brazil
description: A comparatively mild piranha whose teeth carry five cusps, used for cropping seeds, plants and fins rather than flesh. It shoals with its own kind and has an orange throat and anal fin.

region: Amazon, Orinoco & Paraguay basins and the Guianas
description: A specialist scale-eater: its strongly protruding lower jaw gapes open to strike the flanks of other fish and knock off scales, which make up most of its diet. Adults develop elongated front rays in the dorsal and anal fins.

region: Amazon basin & the Guianas
description: A disc-shaped, shimmering silver herbivore that schools nervously in open water. Males develop a longer, red-edged anal fin, and a group will strip a planted tank of soft vegetation.

region: Amazon, Orinoco & Paraguay basins
description: Often sold simply as the silver dollar; it has a steeply rising back and plain, bright silver flanks, and males carry a red-edged anal fin. Schools of these herbivores need open swimming space and plenty of greens.

region: Amazon basin — Brazil
description: A silver dollar marked with fine dark vertical bars across its silver flanks. Like its relatives it is a schooling herbivore that eats soft plants.

region: Amazon basin — Brazil
description: A silver dollar speckled with small dark spots over the upper flank, with an orange-red edge on the male's anal fin. It schools in quiet, vegetated waters and feeds largely on plants.

region: Amazon & Paraguay basins — Brazil, Bolivia & Paraguay
description: Larger, bolder dark spots scattered over the body set this silver dollar apart; breeding males show red in the anal fin. A schooling herbivore that needs a big, open tank.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins — Brazil, Peru, Colombia & Venezuela
description: A large silver dollar with a single broad black vertical bar across the middle of its body, the width varying between individuals and populations. Adults are big, fast schooling herbivores that need a very large tank.

region: Orinoco & Amazon basins and the Guianas
description: Named for the male's red, hook-shaped anal fin edged in black. Adults are silver, often with dark flecks, and form fast-moving schools that devour soft aquarium plants.

region: Amazon, Orinoco & Paraná–Paraguay basins
description: A deep, silvery pacu with a sharply keeled, serrated belly. Large schools migrate through flooded forest feeding on fruits, seeds and plants.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins
description: One of the largest characins, feeding on fruit and seeds that drop into flooded forest and on zooplankton strained with its long gill rakers. Juveniles sold as 'black pacu' quickly outgrow home aquaria and suit only public aquaria.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins
description: Juveniles mimic the red-bellied piranha with a bright red chest, but this pacu has flat, molar-like teeth for crushing fruits, nuts and seeds. It grows far too large for home aquaria, reaching well over half a metre.

region: Paraná–Paraguay & Uruguay basins — Brazil, Paraguay, Bolivia & Argentina
description: The pacu of the Pantanal, which eats fruits and seeds that fall into flooded forest and disperses them along the river. Widely farmed, it is shown in public aquaria featuring Pantanal and Paraná fauna.

region: São Francisco & upper Paraná basins — Brazil
description: A darter-like characin that props itself on its broad pectoral and pelvic fins on stones in flowing water, darting out to snap up small invertebrates. Its sandy body is crossed by dark bars over a dark midlateral stripe.

region: Amazon, Rio Negro & Orinoco basins and the Guianas
description: A secretive micropredator of forest streams with a black spot at the base of the tail. Males grow a huge, flag-like dorsal fin and guard eggs laid on the roof of a cave or under a leaf until the fry swim free.

region: Upper Rio Negro & upper Orinoco — Brazil, Venezuela, Colombia & Peru
description: A tiny crenuchid of shaded, acidic blackwater streams. Males are velvety blue-black with an enormous orange-edged dorsal fin and defend small territories where eggs are laid; females are plain brown.

region: Amazon, Rio Negro & Orinoco basins — Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela & Peru
description: A large, migratory detritivore that rasps algae and organic film from wood and stone with fleshy, sucker-like lips. Its tail and anal fin are boldly striped black and cream, and huge schools leave blackwater tributaries to spawn in silt-laden whitewater rivers.

region: Amazon basin — Peru, Colombia & Brazil
description: Also called the kissing prochilodus for its fleshy, protrusible lips, which work constantly over wood and stone. The black-and-white striped tail gives it its trade name, and the pelvic and anal fins glow orange-red.

region: Paraná–Paraguay, Uruguay & Paraíba do Sul basins — Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay & Uruguay
description: A large migratory detritivore that sucks organic mud from river beds with its protrusible lips and makes up a dominant share of the fish biomass in the lower Paraná. Dark lines run along each scale row on its silvery flanks.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins and the Guianas
description: A slender, fast-swimming shoaler that grazes algae and detritus from submerged surfaces with its small underslung mouth. A black band starts mid-body and runs into the lower half of the tail, with deep red on the tail edge beneath it.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins and the Guianas
description: Named for the 'half stripe' that starts at a round black spot in mid-flank and runs back into the lower tail lobe. Large schools graze algae and detritus in rivers and flooded forest.

region: Amazon basin & the Guianas — Brazil, Guyana, Suriname & French Guiana
description: A silvery shoaling grazer with a single dark, rectangular spot in the middle of each flank and a dark stripe on the lower tail lobe; a mood-dependent grey line can join the two. Like other hemiodids it is a fast, nervous swimmer that needs a long tank and a lid.

region: Amazon, Rio Negro & Orinoco basins — Brazil, Peru, Colombia & Venezuela
description: A pike-like surface predator whose long beak ends in a fleshy flap; it hangs motionless just under the surface before lunging at small fish. Extremely skittish, it will jump or damage its snout on the glass if startled.

region: Rio Negro basin — Brazil & Venezuela
description: A slender, beaked pike characin with a bold black stripe from the snout tip to the tail and dark-spotted fins. Small groups hover near the surface of blackwater streams, ambushing small fish.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins and the Guianas
description: The largest pike characin, a fast hunter of big rivers that can exceed 80 cm in the wild. Silvery with a beaked snout and dark spots on the tail, it is kept mainly in public aquaria.

region: Magdalena, Atrato & Lake Maracaibo basins — Colombia, Venezuela & Panama
description: Also called the hujeta, a slim surface predator with a long, toothy snout and dorsal and anal fins set far back for fast lunges. It floats motionless among plants near the surface before striking small fish.

region: Widespread from Costa Rica to Argentina
description: A thick-bodied ambush predator, also called the wolf fish, that lies motionless on the bottom of swamps and slow rivers and engulfs fish with a sudden lunge. It tolerates very low oxygen and can survive in drying, near-anoxic pools.

region: Guianas & lower Amazon — Tocantins, Xingu & Tapajós basins
description: The giant of the trahiras, approaching a metre in the wild, with a dark spot on the gill cover. A sit-and-wait predator of clear rivers that is kept only in public aquaria and very large private systems.

region: Tropical South America east of the Andes, and Trinidad
description: An air-breathing trahira that gulps air into its vascularised swim bladder, letting it live in stagnant, oxygen-poor swamps. A dark band runs along the flank behind a black, pale-ringed spot on the gill cover.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins and the Guianas
description: A small, cylindrical trahira that gulps air at the surface and hides among roots and leaf litter in forest swamps. Some populations are flushed brick-red, and mature males grow a taller dorsal fin.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins and the Guianas
description: A slim, pointed-headed hunter whose long jaws are lined with fangs, dashing out from cover to seize small fish. It is silver with a black spot at the tail base and a red-tinged tail, and needs live or meaty foods.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins and the Guianas
description: The largest Acestrorhynchus, a sleek silver predator with a fang-lined, pointed snout and a dark spot at the tail base. It hunts fish in the open water of large rivers and flooded forest.

region: Amazon basin — Brazil, Peru, Bolivia & Colombia
description: Also called the payara, named for two huge fangs in the lower jaw that slot into sockets in the upper jaw. A fast-water predator that impales fish on its fangs and needs an enormous tank with strong current.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins and the Guianas
description: The largest payara, exceeding a metre in the wild; a powerful rapids-dwelling predator prized by anglers and shown only in large public aquaria. It has a dark blotch behind the gill cover and a dark-edged tail.

region: Amazon, Orinoco & Paraná–Paraguay basins
description: Also called the dogtooth characin: an extremely elongate, compressed predator with a steeply upturned, fanged mouth that seizes fish from below. Its large pectoral fins and keeled belly give it a distinctive knife-like shape.

region: Congo River basin — Democratic Republic of the Congo
description: Shoals in slow, tannin-stained tributaries of the central Congo basin. Mature males flash a rainbow of blue, gold and violet across their large scales and grow long, feathery dorsal fins and a fringed tail.

region: Niger Delta & coastal rivers of Nigeria
description: Also called Arnold's tetra: a large-scaled, active shoaler of coastal Nigerian rivers with the upper half of each eye bright red and a black blotch in the dorsal fin. Males have a striped red, yellow and black anal fin.

region: West & Central Africa — Gambia to the Congo
description: A large, silvery-gold African tetra with a black stripe on the tail stem that runs into the tail fin and red in the upper half of the eye. Males develop a long, trailing filament on the dorsal fin.

region: Sierra Leone, Liberia & Côte d'Ivoire
description: A tiny West African characin of shaded forest swamps, with a translucent amber body, a fine iridescent line along the flank and red-orange fins. It is very timid and an accomplished jumper.

region: Lower Congo basin — Democratic Republic of the Congo
description: A smaller cousin of the Congo tetra with iridescent silvery-yellow flanks, yellow fins edged in white and a broad dark band through the middle of the tail. Mature males develop white-tipped, extended fins and a long dark central tail streamer.

region: West Africa — Sierra Leone, Liberia, Côte d'Ivoire & Ghana
description: One of the smallest African characins at about 2 cm, a translucent amber fish of shaded forest swamps. Males carry rows of black dots on the rear body and tail stem, while females are plain.

region: West-central Africa — Gabon & Republic of the Congo
description: A slim, active African tetra with a blue-green sheen, red upper eye and a dark stripe through the tail stem into the middle of the tail. Males have longer fins and squabble harmlessly among themselves.

region: Widespread in sub-Saharan Africa — Zambezi, Okavango, Congo, Niger & Nile basins
description: A fast pelagic predator with interlocking, dagger-like teeth, dark lengthwise stripes and a blood-red tail. Shoals hunt in open rivers and lakes; it is shown in large public aquaria.

region: Congo basin & Lake Tanganyika — DR Congo, Angola, Zambia & Tanzania
description: Juveniles are bright orange with six black bars and red fins, a pattern that fades toward dull orange-grey in large adults. A big, powerful herbivore that strips aquarium plants and becomes intolerant of its own kind.

region: Congo basin — DR Congo, Republic of the Congo & Angola
description: A long-snouted Distichodus with an orange-yellow body crossed by about seven dark bars and red fins. It grazes plants and invertebrates, and adults are boisterous and best kept alone in very large tanks.

region: Lower Congo basin — DR Congo
description: A small, plain silver-grey Distichodus with red-tinged fins. Peaceful in groups, but like its larger relatives it eats soft plants.

region: West-central Africa — Cameroon, Gabon & Republic of the Congo
description: A silvery Distichodus with a few dusky vertical marks along the mid-flank, a vertically elongate dark spot at the base of the tail and reddish fins. It is a plant-eating grazer best kept in a small group with robust tankmates.

region: Central Congo basin — DR Congo
description: At about 6 cm the smallest of its genus, with ten dark spots and bars on a golden-brown body and reddish fins. Unlike its giant relatives it suits community tanks, though it nibbles soft-leaved plants.

region: West & Central Africa — Nile, Niger, Volta, Chad & Congo basins
description: A small, hardy African characin with a single black stripe from snout to tail bordered above by a gold line. In spawning condition males flush red on the dorsal fin and upper tail lobe.

region: Congo basin & coastal rivers — Cameroon, Republic of the Congo, DR Congo & Angola
description: A tiny, colourful characin of swampy, plant-choked pools; breeding males glow orange-red beneath an iridescent green back and a dark lateral band. Pairs scatter eggs among fine-leaved plants.

region: Congo basin — DR Congo
description: A small, golden-brown Neolebias with three dark lengthwise lines and red-tinged fins. It lives among dense vegetation in quiet forest waters and is shy in the aquarium.

region: Niger basin & coastal rivers of West Africa
description: An elongate predator with a long, toothed snout that specialises in biting pieces from the fins of other fish. It lurks motionless among plant stems before darting out.

region: Westernmost West Africa — Senegal & Gambia east to the Cavally River, Côte d'Ivoire
description: An ambush predator of vegetated swamps and floodplains that is unusual among characiforms in building a floating foam nest, which the parents guard. Dark bars radiate from the eye across its pike-like head; the Zambezi and Okavango 'African pike' is now H. cuvieri.
